coverage.user_input: I step to the dispatch-box doorway and catch sight of Niko Rell on the loading arcade. I raise an open hand rather than call across the floor. "Niko. Can we talk here a moment? I want to hear what you have to say."

prose:
Niko sees the lifted hand.

For a moment he does nothing. Rain stipples the loading arcade between you, turning the freight floor into a wavering reflection of lamps, boots, and descending steel. He has the look of someone who has already decided which questions he will not answer.

Then he comes as far as the dispatch-box threshold and stops beneath its lintel.

Kessa does not rise from her chair. “This is a Guild-lit room,” she says. “Not a holding pen. He may stand there. He does not enter my conversation unless I ask him to.”

Niko gives her a brief nod, more recognition than apology. His gaze finds yours.

“I don’t have Ora with me,” he says. “I won’t tell you where she is, where she was, or what she kept. Don’t ask.”

He lets that boundary stand before continuing.

“I did see why I thought you ought to know I was here.” He glances over one shoulder into the rain-lit arcade. “A woman in municipal gray spoke to a lift scheduler two bays down. Asked whether an auditor had come out of the memorial hall carrying paper. The scheduler gave her nothing useful. I watched her leave toward the canal stairs.”

The word *municipal* feels oily in this room. It proves no office, no sponsor, no link to Aster or Sol. It proves only that someone was willing to spend an ordinary question on your outline.

“I’m not asking you to follow her,” Niko says. “And I’m not offering you a route to anybody. I’m telling you because people who want a person isolated usually begin by learning which door she used.”

Kessa’s cup clicks softly against its saucer. She has not taken her eyes from you.

“The dead-book waits,” she says. “So does my receipt. Neither becomes less true because the arcade has developed a shadow.”

Niko’s face closes slightly at that, as if he respects the refusal to let fear turn every obligation into an emergency exit. He places an open palm against the doorframe.

“If you sign,” he says, “keep the paper in your own hand until you decide who has earned it. If you don’t, don’t pretend the token has stopped asking.”

Outside, a freight lift begins its slow climb, carrying a cage of sealed containers through the rain-bright shaft. Kessa’s dead-book sheet lies beneath the amber lamp. Beside it, the narrow Wickglass receipt waits blank, a fact not yet bought with the sentence it requires.

Niko remains at the threshold, available for only the kind of conversation he has chosen to permit.

coverage.user_input: "At the shutter you told Ora: west conduit, two turns, then the lift cage. Lose the lane cameras in the condensers." I keep my voice low. "Did that route hold? I am asking you, not writing an answer for you."

prose:
Niko’s eyes narrow at the precision of the question. Outside, rain combs silver lines through the loading arcade; a lift cage rises behind him, slow enough to make every sealed container look accused.

“I told her that route because it was good for the first part of the night,” he says. “It held through the west conduit and the condensers. No lane cameras caught us there. I watched Ora take the second turn.”

He stops. The boundary arrives without performance.

“After that, we separated. Deliberately. I don’t know whether she took the lift cage, doubled back, or found another exit. If I knew it, I wouldn’t give it to you in a dispatch box.”

The answer has less comfort in it than a lie would have. It is also less useful to anyone standing beyond the rain and trying to turn concern into a map.

“You asked whether the route held,” Niko continues. “It held as far as I saw it. I saw no public interdiction, no chase, no distress signal. That is not the same as saying Ora is safe. It means I won’t invent an ending because you need one.”

Kessa reaches beneath the dead-book sheet for her satchel. A small indicator on its clasp pulses once: an incoming welfare inquiry, ordinary Guild routing, unread. She glances at it, then turns the clasp facedown.

“Your friend has given you an honest limit,” she says. “Now give the dead the same courtesy.”

Niko looks at the sheet bearing Nera Voss’s name. His expression does not soften, but it loses some of its defensive set.

“You can keep asking me what I saw,” he says. “You cannot make me carry Ora’s half of the world into this room.”

Under the amber lamp, the dead-book sentence waits in Mara’s own hand or remains unwritten. Beside it, the Wickglass receipt remains a narrow, conditional piece of truth: an unnamed municipal adjunct asked how to isolate carriers through family obligations; Wickglass refused the question. Beyond the glass, the municipal-gray stranger is still only rain, a scheduler’s recollection, and a direction toward canal stairs.

Kessa slides the pen toward you. It rolls once and comes to rest against the bronze token.

coverage.user_input: At the loading arcade I see Ora Pell near the conduit access. I stop short of crowding her and keep my hands in view. "Ora. If you are willing, I would like a word. Here, on your side of the doorway."

prose:
Niko’s attention cuts past you.

At the far end of the loading arcade, where the conduit access is recessed beneath a yellow maintenance hood, Ora Pell stands with one shoulder against the jamb. She has changed out of whatever rain gear she wore on the west-conduit leg; her coat is too large through the shoulders and dry only in patches. In one hand she holds a paper cup gone white with steam. A small pleasure, purchased somewhere anonymous, and apparently the only thing in the station she is prepared to let remain simple.

She hears you. Of course she does.

For several seconds she does not come closer. The rain drapes the space between the dispatch box and the conduit door in wavering strands, and the freight lifts make their slow, indifferent ascent behind the glass.

Niko does not turn toward her. He keeps his place at the threshold, but his voice is pitched for you alone.

“Her being there doesn’t amend anything I said.”

“I know,” Ora says.

Her answer is flat, not cruel. She lifts the cup, takes a careful sip, then pushes herself off the jamb. She crosses only far enough to stand on the arcade side of the doorway, exactly where you asked. Her gaze touches Niko first, a brief confirmation between people who have survived the usefulness of not knowing too much. Then it settles on you.

“You get one question,” she says. “Not about the receipt. Not about where I’ve been. Not about where I go after this.”

Her eyes flick to Kessa’s table, to the dead-book sheet under its amber lamp, and back.

“And you don’t get to turn seeing me into proof that anybody’s safe. I stopped for tea. That’s all you can honestly say.”

Kessa leaves the pen where it rests against the bronze token. Her unread Guild indicator pulses once beneath the overturned clasp and goes dark again.

“Nera Voss is still dead,” she says. “Your sentence is still yours.”

Ora’s mouth tightens at that, perhaps in recognition, perhaps simply because she has spent enough of the night watching people try to make urgency outrank consequence.

“You wanted a word,” she tells you. “Spend it carefully.”

Rain whispers over the conduit door. Niko remains between the dispatch house and the rest of the arcade, offering neither endorsement nor interference. On the table, the dead-book waits beside the conditional Wickglass receipt: one narrow account of a refused inquiry into isolating carriers through family obligations, purchasable only at the price Kessa named.

Ora holds her cup in both hands and waits without yielding an inch of the boundary she has drawn.

prose:
Ora looks down into her tea. The cup has softened at the seam beneath her fingers; a dark crescent has formed on the concrete below it.

“You caught the tin,” she says. “You did what was needed in that second. That wasn’t nothing.”

Her eyes rise to yours, guarded but present.

“But a rescue story has a shape people like. It gives somebody a rescuer, somebody rescued, and a clean reason to start asking who owes whom afterward. It lets the person who held the door call the next door theirs to choose.”

Niko’s jaw shifts once. He does not dispute her.

“I needed to get out of that bay,” Ora continues. “Niko helped me get out. You caught what I dropped. None of that bought either of you the rest of my night. It doesn’t make my half of the receipt communal property. It doesn’t make me proof that the route was good, or that I’m safe, or that you did enough.”

The freight lift behind the glass reaches a higher deck with a muffled mechanical thud. Rain veils the cage as it opens somewhere above.

“If you want to understand it now,” Ora says, “understand that I left because I chose to leave, and I stopped here because I chose to stop. Tomorrow, I may choose something else. Don’t turn that into a debt you can collect, or a protection claim you can make over me.”

Her gaze flicks toward Kessa’s table.

“And don’t use my being upright to escape what Nera Voss is asking of you. We’ve all watched enough people call their fear urgent so they don’t have to call their harm by its name.”

Kessa does not reach for the dead-book. She merely turns the pen a quarter-turn on the tabletop.

“Plainly put,” she says.

Niko steps back from the threshold, granting Ora the little corridor of space her words have made. “You heard her,” he says. “No route. No receipt. No custody dressed up as concern.”

Ora takes one final sip, then lowers the cup. “That was your one question.”

For an instant her expression eases, though it never becomes trust.

“Make the next thing you do yours,” she says. “Not mine.”

Amber light holds on the dead-book sheet and the bronze token. Beyond the dispatch-box glass, rain turns the loading arcade into a hundred blurred exits.
